title: SSH Key Management
description: Generate, configure, and manage SSH keys for secure Git authentication.

data.text: SSH keys provide passwordless, cryptographically secure authentication to Git remotes. Each key pair consists of a private key (kept secret on your machine) and a public key (added to GitHub, GitLab, or your Git server). Proper key management prevents unauthorized access and simplifies automation.
Use ssh-keygen to generate a new key pair. Use Ed25519 for modern systems; use RSA 4096 for compatibility with older systems.

data.title: Generate an Ed25519 SSH key
data.code:
# Generate a new Ed25519 key pair
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your-email@example.com"

# Output:
# Generating public/private ed25519 key pair.
# Enter file in which to save the key (/c/Users/you/.ssh/id_ed25519):
# Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase):
# Enter same passphrase again:

# Key files created:
# ~/.ssh/id_ed25519       (private key — NEVER share this)
# ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub   (public key — safe to share)

# For older systems without Ed25519 support:
ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "your-email@example.com"

data.text: Copy your public key and add it to your GitHub account. GitHub uses the public key to verify your identity when you authenticate via SSH.

data.title: Copy and add SSH key to GitHub
data.code:
# Copy the public key to clipboard
# Windows:
clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# macOS:
pbcopy < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Linux:
xclip -sel clip < ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Or view and copy manually
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Add to GitHub:
# Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key → paste → Add SSH key

# Test the connection
ssh -T git@github.com

# Output:
# Hi your-username! You've successfully authenticated, but GitHub does not provide shell access.

data.text: If you use multiple GitHub accounts (personal and work) or multiple Git servers, configure ~/.ssh/config to route connections to the correct key.

data.title: SSH config for multiple accounts
data.code:
# ~/.ssh/config

# Personal GitHub account
Host github-personal
  HostName github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_personal
  IdentitiesOnly yes

# Work GitHub account
Host github-work
  HostName github.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_work
  IdentitiesOnly yes

# Company Git server
Host git.company.com
  HostName git.company.com
  User git
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_work
  IdentitiesOnly yes

# Use in remote URLs:
# git@github-personal:username/project.git
# git@github-work:company/project.git

data.text: The SSH agent caches your passphrase so you do not enter it for every Git operation. Start the agent and add your key at the beginning of your session.

data.title: Start SSH agent and add key
data.code:
# Start the SSH agent (add to your shell profile)
eval "$(ssh-agent -s)"

# Add your key to the agent
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

# List loaded keys
ssh-add -l

# Remove a key from the agent
ssh-add -d ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

data.text: Rotate SSH keys periodically and immediately if you suspect compromise. Remove old keys from GitHub and your SSH config. Generate new keys and add them before removing old ones to avoid lockout.

data.title: Rotate SSH keys safely
data.code:
# Step 1: Generate new key
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your-email@example.com" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_new

# Step 2: Add new public key to GitHub
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_new.pub
# Add via GitHub web UI

# Step 3: Test new key
ssh -T git@github.com

# Step 4: Remove old key from GitHub
# GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → Delete old key

# Step 5: Update SSH config
# Change IdentityFile to new key

# Step 6: Remove old key file
rm ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_old

data.title: Never commit private SSH keys
data.text: Private SSH keys are sensitive credentials. If committed to Git, they must be treated as compromised: rotate the key immediately and remove it from the repository history with git filter-branch or BFG Repo-Cleaner.

items.question: Can I use the same SSH key for multiple services?
items.answer: Yes, but it is better to use separate keys for different services. If one key is compromised, you only need to rotate it for that service.

items.question: What is the difference between Ed25519 and RSA?
items.answer: Ed25519 is faster, produces shorter keys, and is more secure than RSA. Use Ed25519 for new keys. Use RSA only for compatibility with older systems.

items.question: How do I back up my SSH keys?
items.answer: Back up ~/.ssh/ to an encrypted location (e.g., password manager, encrypted USB). Without your private key, you lose access to all servers that use it.

items.question: Can I use a hardware token (YubiKey) for SSH?
items.answer: Yes. YubiKeys and other hardware tokens support SSH key storage. The private key never leaves the hardware, providing stronger security than software keys.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use ssh-keygen -t ed25519 to generate modern SSH keys
Add your public key to GitHub via Settings → SSH and GPG keys
Configure ~/.ssh/config for multiple keys and accounts
Use ssh-agent to cache your passphrase during your session
Rotate keys regularly and never commit private keys
